sources.title: Operating Systems Lecture Notes (Prof. S. Rao)
Modern Operating Systems in Practice, 3rd Ed.
JD: Site Reliability Engineer, Platform Team

processes.name: Processes
processes.description: A process is a program in execution that owns its own address space, registers, and state information.

threads.name: Threads
threads.description: Threads are the smallest units of CPU scheduling within a process that share code and data but maintain independent stacks.

cpu_scheduling.name: CPU Scheduling
cpu_scheduling.description: Algorithms that determine which process or thread receives CPU time, including strategies like FCFS and Round Robin.

synchronization.name: Process Synchronization
synchronization.description: Mechanisms such as semaphores used to coordinate access to shared resources and prevent race conditions.

deadlocks.name: Deadlocks
deadlocks.description: A system state where processes wait indefinitely for resources, occurring when specific conditions are met simultaneously.

memory_management.name: Memory Management
memory_management.description: Techniques like paging that map logical memory to physical memory using fixed-size frames and pages.

virtual_memory.name: Virtual Memory
virtual_memory.description: A mechanism that allows processes to use more logical memory than physical memory, using demand paging and replacement algorithms.

system_startup.name: System Startup
system_startup.description: The initialization process of an operating system, starting from the kernel to the first user-space process.

containers.name: Containers
containers.description: Isolated user-space environments that share a host kernel using namespaces and control groups for resource limits.

claims.statement: A process consists of a program counter, registers, and its own address space during execution.
claims.quote: A process is a program in execution, with its own address space, program counter, registers and open files.

claims.statement: The operating system tracks process information using a Process Control Block.
claims.quote: The operating system keeps information about each process in a process control block (PCB).

claims.statement: Creating a thread is more efficient than a process because it does not require a new address space.
claims.quote: Creating a thread is cheaper than creating a process because no new address space is needed.

claims.statement: The convoy effect describes how FCFS scheduling forces short jobs to wait behind long ones.
claims.quote: First-Come First-Served (FCFS) scheduling can make short jobs wait behind long ones, which is called the convoy effect.

claims.statement: The Linux kernel historically utilized an O(1) scheduler for picking tasks in constant time.
claims.quote: The Linux kernel uses the O(1) scheduler, which picks the next task in constant time using priority arrays.

claims.statement: A race condition occurs when thread results depend on the specific order of accessing shared data.
claims.quote: A race condition happens when the result depends on the order in which threads access shared data.

claims.statement: Semaphores are implemented as integer variables manipulated exclusively through atomic wait and signal operations.
claims.quote: A semaphore is an integer variable accessed only through the atomic operations wait and signal.

claims.statement: Four conditions (mutual exclusion, hold and wait, no preemption, circular wait) must be met simultaneously for deadlock.
claims.quote: A deadlock can occur only if four conditions hold at the same time: mutual exclusion, hold and wait, no preemption and circular wait.

claims.statement: Paging eliminates external fragmentation but leaves internal fragmentation in the final page of a process.
claims.quote: Paging removes external fragmentation but can still cause internal fragmentation in the last page.

claims.statement: Belady's anomaly is when increasing the number of frames causes an increase in page faults with FIFO.
claims.quote: With FIFO page replacement, adding more frames can sometimes increase the number of page faults; this is called Belady's anomaly.

claims.statement: Legacy Linux systems started services via SysV init, which ran as the first process with PID 1.
claims.quote: Linux runs SysV init as the first process with PID 1, which starts services using runlevel scripts.

claims.statement: Threads within a single process share the same address space, meaning one thread's error can corrupt shared data.
claims.quote: Threads of the same process share one address space, so a bug in one thread can corrupt data used by the others.

claims.statement: The Completely Fair Scheduler (CFS) replaced the O(1) scheduler in Linux kernel version 2.6.23.
claims.quote: Linux replaced the O(1) scheduler with the Completely Fair Scheduler (CFS) in kernel 2.6.23, released in 2007.

claims.statement: The EEVDF scheduler became the default for normal tasks in Linux kernel 6.6, replacing CFS.
claims.quote: Since Linux 6.6, released in 2023, the EEVDF scheduler has replaced CFS as the default scheduler for normal tasks.

claims.statement: Disrupting one of the four deadlock conditions, such as using lock ordering to prevent circular wait, is sufficient to prevent deadlock.
claims.quote: Breaking any one of the four conditions, for example by ordering locks to prevent circular wait, prevents deadlock.

claims.statement: LRU and the optimal algorithm are stack algorithms that avoid the phenomenon known as Belady's anomaly.
claims.quote: Stack algorithms such as LRU and the optimal algorithm never suffer from Belady's anomaly.

claims.statement: Modern Linux distributions typically utilize systemd as the init system for managing parallel service startup.
claims.quote: Most major Linux distributions now use systemd as the init system that runs as PID 1 and starts services in parallel.

claims.statement: Linux containers restrict resources and isolate processes by using namespaces and control groups (cgroups).
claims.quote: Linux containers isolate processes using namespaces and limit their CPU and memory using control groups (cgroups).

claims.statement: Containers have faster startup times than virtual machines because they share the host's kernel rather than booting a new one.
claims.quote: A container shares the host kernel, so it starts much faster than a virtual machine that boots its own kernel.

claims.statement: Threads of the same process have separate address spaces, making them safer than processes.
claims.quote: Threads of the same process have separate address spaces, which is why threads are safer than processes.

claims.statement: Deadlock requires only two conditions to exist: mutual exclusion and hold and wait.
claims.quote: Deadlock needs only two conditions: mutual exclusion and hold and wait.

claims.statement: Increasing the number of frames in a system always reduces page faults regardless of the replacement algorithm used.
claims.quote: Adding more frames to a process always reduces its page faults, whatever replacement algorithm is used.

claims.statement: Round Robin is the optimal scheduling algorithm that students should always choose for exams.
claims.quote: Round Robin is always the best scheduling algorithm, so always choose it in exams.

claims.statement: Backend roles require expertise in concurrency, including specific knowledge of locks and deadlock avoidance techniques.
claims.quote: Strong understanding of processes, threads and concurrency, including locks and deadlock avoidance.

claims.statement: Backend engineers must know how virtual memory and paging mechanisms influence application performance.
claims.quote: Knowledge of virtual memory and how paging affects application performance.

claims.statement: Practical experience with Linux containers, specifically namespaces and cgroups, is a required skill for infrastructure roles.
claims.quote: Hands-on experience with Linux containers, including namespaces and cgroups.

claims.statement: Proficiency in how the Linux CPU scheduler allocates time between various services is required for this role.
claims.quote: Familiarity with how the Linux CPU scheduler shares CPU time between services.

claims.statement: SRE roles require managing Linux services specifically using systemd as the process with PID 1.
claims.quote: Managing Linux services with systemd, which runs as PID 1 on our servers.

claims.statement: Site Reliability Engineers must be capable of diagnosing memory pressure, page faults, and swapping on active systems.
claims.quote: Diagnosing memory pressure, page faults and swapping on busy machines.

prerequisites.reason: System startup initializes the kernel and creates the first user-space process, building on the concept of a process.
A thread is the smallest unit within a process, so one must understand processes first.
Memory management techniques map the logical memory of a process to physical memory.
Containers are essentially isolated collections of processes and threads sharing the host kernel.
Synchronization mechanisms are used to coordinate access to shared resources between threads within a process.
Scheduling algorithms determine which process or thread gets CPU time, requiring understanding of both units.
Deadlocks occur when synchronization mechanisms (like locks) cause processes to wait indefinitely for resources.
Virtual memory extends memory management with demand paging and replacement algorithms to use more logical than physical memory.
